Their bodies were dismembered and the parts sent to towns of the region for display. The involvement of women in such risings shocked the Spanish authorities, who gave them the same penalties as men.
michelangelo: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was born on 6 March 1475 in Caprese, near Arezzo in Tuscany, where his father Ludovico was the town's judicial administrator. The family had for generations been small-scale bankers in Florence, but the bank failed. Several months after his birth they returned to Florence. After his mother's death in 1481 he lived with a nanny and her husband, a stonecutter, in Settignano, where his father owned a marble quarry and a small farm. He later said he received the knack of handling chisel and hammer with the milk of his nurse.

Michelangelo achieved fame early, and two of his best-known works, the Pietà and David, were sculpted before he was 30. Born in the Republic of Florence, he was mostly active in Rome from his thirties onward. Although he did not consider himself a painter, he created the scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and The Last Judgment on its altar wall, two of the most influential frescoes in Western art.

His design of the Laurentian Library pioneered Mannerist architecture. At 71 he succeeded Antonio da Sangallo the Younger as architect of St. Peter's Basilica, and he changed the plan so that the western end was finished to his design, as was the dome, with some modification after his death on 18 February 1564. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime: Giorgio Vasari's Lives of 1550 called him divino, and Ascanio Condivi's Life of 1553 was prepared with his participation.

The Madonna of the Stairs is his earliest known work in marble, carved in shallow relief. His Bacchus, a commission with a set subject, has the traditional wine cup, vine wreath and fawn, but shows the god with bleary eyes and an unsteady stance. In the Madonna of Bruges the Christ Child, held by his mother's hand, is about to step off into the world. His contemporaries admired his terribilità, the ability to instil awe in those who saw his art.

He wrote more than three hundred sonnets and madrigals. He was a devout Catholic whose faith deepened at the end of his life. Attempts by later artists to imitate the expressive physicality of his style helped bring about Mannerism. The dome of St. Peter's influenced church building for centuries, including St Paul's Cathedral in London, and his unfinished giants for the tomb of Pope Julius II had a deep effect on sculptors such as Rodin and Henry Moore.
middle-ages: The term Middle Ages first appears in Latin in 1469 as media tempestas, middle season. Other early variants were medium aevum, first recorded in 1604, and media saecula, first recorded in 1625. Medieval writers divided history into periods such as the Six Ages or the Four Empires and considered their own time the last before the end of the world. In the 1330s the Italian humanist Petrarch called the post-Roman centuries dark compared with the light of classical antiquity. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use a tripartite periodisation, in 1442, and it became standard after the 17th-century German historian Christoph Cellarius divided history into ancient, medieval and modern.

In the history of Europe the Middle Ages lasted approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries and are divided into the Early, High and Late Middle Ages. They began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Between the 5th and 8th centuries peoples such as the Ostrogoths under Theoderic the Great, the Burgundians and the Franks filled the political void. The break with classical antiquity was incomplete: the new kingdoms kept Roman institutions, and the Byzantine Empire survived in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In the High Middle Ages, which began after 1000, the population of Europe grew from an estimated 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347. Manorialism and feudalism organised society, the East–West Schism came in 1054, and the Crusades were first preached in 1095. The Late Middle Ages brought the Great Famine of 1315–1317 and, from 1347 to 1350, the Black Death, which killed probably about 35 million people, around one-third of Europeans.

The medieval period is often caricatured as a time of ignorance and superstition. The caricature descends from the Renaissance, whose scholars saw the Middle Ages as a decline from the Classical world, and from the Enlightenment, whose scholars saw reason as superior to faith. Others argue that reason was held in high regard in the period.

It is untrue that everyone in the Middle Ages believed the Earth was flat. Lecturers in medieval universities commonly argued that the evidence showed the Earth to be a sphere, and Lindberg and Numbers state that scarcely a Christian scholar of the period failed to acknowledge its sphericity.
middle-east: The Middle East is a geopolitical region generally defined as all of Egypt and all of West Asia except the Caucasus. It roughly corresponds with what Western Europe historically called the Near East, set against the Far East. Its main features are the Arabian Peninsula, Anatolia, the Levant and Mesopotamia, which together make up the Fertile Crescent, and the Iranian plateau. Most of it is hot and arid, but rivers such as the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Jordan irrigate farmland.

The term may have originated with the India Office of the United Kingdom in the 1850s. It became widely known after the American naval strategist Alfred Thayer Mahan used it in 1902 for the area between Arabia and India, in an article on the Persian Gulf. Until the Second World War the area centred on Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean was usually called the Near East.

The Middle East was the first region outside Africa to be settled by modern humans and the first in which writing systems developed. Agriculture was independently developed there and spread during the Neolithic to Europe, the Indus Valley and eastern Africa. The earliest civilisations, Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia in Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt, arose in the Fertile Crescent and the Nile Valley. They were followed by the Hittite, Greek, Hurrian and Urartian civilisations of Asia Minor, Elam, Persia and Media in Iran, and the Levantine civilisations of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit, Canaan, Phoenicia and Israel.

The Near East was first largely unified under the Neo Assyrian Empire, then under the Achaemenid Empire, followed by the Macedonian Empire and, to some degree, by the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire. The Romans stationed five or six legions in the region to defend it from Sasanian and Bedouin raids and invasions. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all originated in the region and have their holiest sites there, as do Manichaeism, Yezidi, the Druze faith and Mandeanism.

Arabs are the largest ethnic group, followed by Iranian and Turkic peoples, with Kurds, Jews, Assyrians and many others. The six languages with most speakers are Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Kurdish, Modern Hebrew and Greek. The Gulf Arab states hold vast reserves of petroleum.
miguel-de-cervantes: Many details of Cervantes's life remain uncertain, including his name, background and appearance. He signed his name as Cerbantes, but his printers used Cervantes, which became the common form. In later life he used Saavedra, the name of a distant relative, rather than Cortinas, after his mother. It is generally accepted that he was born around 29 September 1547 in Alcalá de Henares, the second son of the barber-surgeon Rodrigo de Cervantes and Leonor de Cortinas.

Rodrigo was often in debt or looking for work, and the family moved constantly. When he was imprisoned for debt from October 1553 to April 1554, Leonor supported the family alone. They lived in Córdoba until 1556, when his grandfather died. It has been suggested that one or both parents were New Christians, Catholics of Jewish ancestry, but the view has no wide following. No authenticated portrait of Cervantes is known to exist.

In 1569 Cervantes was forced to leave Spain and went to Rome, where he worked in a cardinal's household. In 1570 he enlisted in a Spanish Navy infantry regiment. He was badly wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571. Captured by Barbary pirates in 1575 while serving as a soldier, he was ransomed after five years and returned to Madrid.

He claimed to have written more than 20 plays, such as El trato de Argel, based on his captivity, but such works were short-lived. His first significant novel, the pastoral romance La Galatea, appeared in 1585 and received little notice. He worked as a purchasing agent and later as a government tax collector. By 1605 he had not been published for 20 years.

Don Quixote, first published in January 1605, set out explicitly to undermine vain and empty chivalric romances. Its portrayal of real life and its everyday speech were considered innovative, and it was instantly popular: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza appeared in masquerades celebrating the birth of Philip IV on 8 April 1605. An unauthorised sequel under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda came out in 1614, and Cervantes published his own second part in 1615. The first part is more comic, the second more sophisticated, with greater depth of characterisation.

His other works include the twelve Novelas ejemplares of 1613, the allegorical poem Viaje del Parnaso, eight short farces, and Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda, published after his death in 1617. English writers rediscovered him in the mid-18th century, and John Bowle published an annotated edition of Don Quixote in 1781. It has been translated into all major languages.
mikhail-gorbachev: Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in Privolnoye, in North Caucasus Krai, into a poor peasant family of Russian and Ukrainian heritage. His parents named him Viktor, but at his mother's insistence he was secretly baptised Mikhail. At three he moved to the collective farm that his maternal grandfather, a Communist Party member since 1928, chaired. He studied at Moscow State University, married fellow student Raisa Titarenko in 1953 and took his law degree in 1955. In Stavropol he worked for the Komsomol and supported Khrushchev's de-Stalinization. He became first party secretary of the Stavropol Regional Committee in 1970, and in 1978 returned to Moscow as a secretary of the Central Committee.

On 11 March 1985 the Politburo elected Gorbachev general secretary after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He wished to preserve the Soviet state and its Marxist-Leninist principles but held that significant reform was needed. His glasnost, or openness, widened freedom of speech and the press, and perestroika, restructuring, sought to decentralise economic decision-making. He withdrew troops from the Soviet-Afghan War and met United States president Ronald Reagan at the Reykjavik Summit to discuss limiting nuclear weapons and ending the Cold War.

The elected Congress of People's Deputies that he formed undermined the party's supremacy. When Warsaw Pact countries abandoned Marxist-Leninist rule in 1989 he declined to intervene militarily, and in November East Germany opened the Berlin Wall, a decision he praised. German reunification followed in 1990, and many observers then declared the Cold War over. He received the Nobel Peace Prize that year.

Growing nationalism in the republics threatened to break up the Soviet Union, and in August 1991 hardliners launched an unsuccessful coup against him. In its wake the union dissolved, against his wishes. Out of office he launched the Gorbachev Foundation in 1992 and Green Cross International in 1993. He died in Moscow on 30 August 2022, aged 91. Many, particularly in Western countries, praise his role in ending the Cold War and tolerating the fall of Marxist-Leninist governments in central and eastern Europe, while critics hold that he weakened Russia's global influence and precipitated an economic collapse.
milan: Milan lies in the north-western part of the Po Valley, roughly halfway between the river Po to the south and the foothills of the Alps, with the lakes Como, Maggiore and Lugano to the north, the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east. The land is flat, and the highest point is 122 m above sea level. The Celtic name Medhelanon, later Latinized as Mediolanum, is usually explained as a settlement in the midst of the plain, or between watercourses, given the Olona, Lambro and Seveso rivers.

According to the account of Livy, the Gaulish king Ambicatus sent his nephew Bellovesus into northern Italy, and Bellovesus is said to have founded the settlement in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus. Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres, belonging to the Golasecca culture, settled the site as Medhelanon, around a sanctuary in the shape of an ellipse with axes of 443 m and 323 m, near the present Piazza della Scala. The Romans conquered the city in 222 BCE. From 284 to 402 CE it was capital of the western part of the Roman Empire.

In the late fourth century Saint Ambrose, as bishop of Milan, reshaped the centre and built the great basilicas at the city gates: Sant'Ambrogio, San Nazaro in Brolo, San Simpliciano and Sant'Eustorgio, which still stand. In the Late Middle Ages the wealthy Duchy of Milan was one of the great forces behind the Renaissance, and the Visconti family, major patrons of the arts, made the city a centre of Gothic art. Work on the cathedral began in 1386 and ended in 1877. Leonardo da Vinci worked in Milan from 1482 until 1499 and painted the Virgin of the Rocks and The Last Supper there.

In the early modern period Milan was a major centre of the Italian Enlightenment, and its cultural and political struggle against Austrian domination was crucial in the reunification of the Kingdom of Italy. From the 19th century the city led the industrial and financial development of Italy. After the Second World War its population grew with migration, first from poorer and rural parts of Italy and later from abroad, and it peaked at 1,743,427 in 1973.

Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the second-largest city in Italy after Rome, with a population of 1,362,863. It is regarded as the country's industrial and financial centre and is a world centre of fashion. The Cathedral, the largest church in Italy, the Pinacoteca di Brera and the Castello Sforzesco, which holds Michelangelo's last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà, are among its principal monuments. Of the Roman city, few remains survive, notably the Colonne di San Lorenzo.
minnesota: Minnesota is the northernmost contiguous state, since the isolated Northwest Angle in Lake of the Woods County is the only part of the 48 contiguous states north of the 49th parallel. It borders Manitoba and Ontario to the north, Wisconsin to the east, Iowa to the south and North Dakota and South Dakota to the west. It is known as the Land of 10,000 Lakes, with 14,420 bodies of fresh water of at least ten acres each. About a third of the state is forested, and much of the rest is prairie and farmland.

The name comes from the Dakota name for the Minnesota River, either mní sóta, clear blue water, or Mníssota, cloudy water. The state seal carries the phrase Mni Sóta Makoce, the land where the water reflects the skies.

Native Americans have lived in Minnesota since the Woodland period of the 11th century BCE. The Upper Mississippian culture, made up of the Oneota and other Siouan speakers, emerged around 1000 CE and lasted until Europeans arrived in the 17th century. The Dakota lived in what is now Minnesota when French voyageurs and fur traders arrived, using the Grand Portage to reach trapping areas. The Anishinaabe, also called Ojibwe or Chippewa, were migrating in and formed an alliance with the Dakota. European powers destabilised the region, the alliance collapsed, and the Dakota-Ojibwe War followed.

The region was part of Spanish Louisiana from 1762 to 1802. The part east of the Mississippi became part of the United States at the end of the American Revolutionary War, and the part to the west came with the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Territory of Minnesota was formed in 1849, with Saint Paul as its capital, and Minnesota was admitted as the 32nd state in 1858. Its motto, L'Étoile du Nord, The Star of the North, is the only state motto in French.

Settlers came from across the country, and growth was based first on timber, agriculture and railroad construction. Into the early 20th century European immigrants arrived in large numbers, particularly from Scandinavia, Germany and Central Europe. The state was at the forefront of labour rights, women's suffrage and political reform.

Saint Paul is the capital and Minneapolis the most populous city, and the two form the Twin Cities, where more than half the state's people live. Minnesota has 11 federally recognised Native American reservations, seven Ojibwe and four Dakota, and its culture reflects Scandinavian and German influence.
minsk: Minsk stands on the southeastern slope of the Minsk Hills, on the Svislach River and the now subterranean Nyamiha, at an average altitude of 220 metres. The Svislach flows through an ancient river valley formed by meltwater at the end of the last Ice Age, and six smaller rivers lie within the city limits. The city was first built on the hills, which allowed defensive fortifications, and its western parts are still the most hilly. Pine and mixed forests border its north and east, and the Zaslawskaye reservoir, built in 1956 and known as the Minsk sea, lies five kilometres from its north-western edge.

The Svislach valley was the boundary between two early East Slavic tribes, the Krivichs and the Dregoviches, and by 980 it was part of the Principality of Polotsk. The Primary Chronicle mentions the settlement as Měneskъ for the year 1067, in connection with the Battle on the River Nemiga. That year is now widely accepted as the founding date, and city authorities give 3 March 1067, though the town already had wooden walls and must have existed for some time. Kiev annexed the Principality of Minsk in 1129, the Polotsk dynasty regained it in 1146, and by 1150 Minsk rivalled Polotsk as the major city of the former principality.

The city was later annexed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and received town privileges in 1499. From 1569 it was the capital of Minsk Voivodeship in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Polish rule brought a massive migration of Jews to Belarusian lands. Minsk passed to the Russian Empire in 1793 after the Second Partition of Poland. In 1897 Jews were the largest religious group, 47,562 of 90,912 residents. From 1919 to 1991 it was the capital of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, a republic of the Soviet Union from 1922.

Minsk is the capital and largest city of Belarus, with a special administrative status and a population of about two million. Since 1991 it has been the capital of the independent Republic of Belarus. The city is divided into nine districts. Among its historic churches are the Orthodox Cathedral of the Holy Spirit, a former Bernardine convent church, and the Cathedral of Saint Mary, built by the Jesuits. Its first theatres and libraries date from the middle of the 19th century.
mir-osman-ali-khan: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.
moamoria-rebellion: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.
mohamed-amin-didi: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.
moldova: Moldova is a landlocked country of 33,843 km2 between the Prut river on the west, which separates it from Romania, and the Dniester on the east. Most of it is hilly, with elevations that never exceed 430 metres, the highest point being the Bălănești Hill, and exceptionally rich Chernozem soil covers around three-quarters of the land. About 88% of the area lies in the Bessarabia region, and a narrow strip on the east bank of the Dniester is in the unrecognised breakaway state of Transnistria.

In 1999 Moldova acquired from Ukraine a 0.45 kilometre frontage on the Danube, which turned the village of Giurgiulești into a river port. The name comes from the Moldova River; a legend recounted by the chroniclers Dimitrie Cantemir and Grigore Ureche says that Prince Dragoș named it after his hound Molda, which drowned there.

In antiquity the area was a crossroads for invasions by the Scythians, Goths, Huns and other tribes, followed by periods of Roman and Byzantine control. The Principality of Moldavia emerged in the 1350s, reached prominence under rulers such as Stephen the Great, and was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire from 1538. In 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the eastern half to the Russian Empire, which called it Bessarabia. Southern Bessarabia was returned to Moldavia in 1856, three years before Moldavia united with Wallachia to form Romania, but Russia restored its rule over the entire region in 1878.

Bessarabia declared independence in February 1918 and joined Romania later that year after a vote of its assembly, a decision disputed by Soviet Russia. In 1940, as a consequence of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Romania was compelled to cede Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union, which created the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. It declared independence on 27 August 1991 and took the name Moldova, and the Transnistria War of 1992 left the breakaway region de facto independent.

Moldova adopted its constitution in 1994 and is a parliamentary republic with a 101-seat unicameral parliament. It was granted European Union candidate status in June 2022. The population was an estimated 2,423,300, and ethnic Moldovans were almost 77% of it in the census.
moliere: Molière was born in Paris and baptised as Jean Poquelin on 15 January 1622, the first son of Jean Poquelin and Marie Cressé, from a prosperous bourgeois family. He lost his mother at 10. His father bought the post of valet of the King's chamber and keeper of carpets and upholstery in 1631, and the son took it over in 1641. He studied at the Jesuit Collège de Clermont and around 1642 as a provincial lawyer, though it is not documented that he qualified. In June 1643 he left his social class for the stage, joined the actress Madeleine Béjart, and founded the Illustre Théâtre.

Thirteen years as an itinerant actor refined his comic skill, and he began to write, combining commedia dell'arte elements with the more refined French comedy. Through aristocratic patrons, including Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, brother of Louis XIV, he gained a command performance before the King at the Louvre. He was granted the grande salle of the Petit-Bourbon and later the theatre in the Palais-Royal, where plays such as The Affected Ladies, The School for Husbands and The School for Wives succeeded. His troupe received a royal pension and the title Troupe du Roi.

His satires drew criticism. The Catholic Church in France denounced Tartuffe, a study of religious hypocrisy, and the Parlement banned it, while Don Juan was withdrawn and never restaged by Molière. His other plays include The Misanthrope, The Miser and The Learned Ladies. His health suffered from the work, and by 1667 he had to take a break from the stage.

Molière suffered from pulmonary tuberculosis. On 17 February 1673, while playing Argan in his last play, The Imaginary Invalid, he collapsed in a fit of coughing and haemorrhage. He finished the performance, collapsed again, and died at home a few hours later without the last rites: two priests refused to come and a third arrived too late. As actors could not then be buried in consecrated ground, his widow Armande asked the King for a normal funeral at night, and he was buried in the part of the cemetery reserved for unbaptised infants. In 1817 his remains were moved to Père Lachaise Cemetery.

He is considered the creator of modern French comedy. A tartuffe is a hypocrite, and a harpagon, after the miser of The Miser, is an obsessively greedy man. His works were translated into English prose by John Ozell in 1714, and the first complete English version, by Baker and Miller, appeared in 1739.
mongolia: Mongolia is a landlocked country between Russia to the north and China to the south, with an area of 1,564,116 square kilometres. Its landscape is grassy steppe, mountains in the north and west, and the Gobi Desert in the south, and the whole country is part of the Mongolian Plateau. The highest point is Khüiten Peak, at 4,374 metres. The climate is high, cold and windy, with long winters, and Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest capital city. The country is subject to harsh conditions known as zud, in which large numbers of livestock die from starvation or freezing.

The Khoit Tsenkher Cave holds paintings dated to 20,000 years ago, and Neolithic agricultural settlements from about 5500 to 3500 BCE predate horse-riding nomadism, which became the dominant culture. The territory was ruled by nomadic empires, among them the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Rouran Khaganate, the First Turkic Khaganate, the Second Turkic Khaganate and the Uyghur Khaganate. In 1206 Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered China proper and established the Yuan dynasty. After the Yuan collapsed, the Mongols retreated to Mongolia and resumed factional conflict, except in the era of Dayan Khan and Tumen Zasagt Khan.

Tibetan Buddhism spread to Mongolia in the 16th century, and by the early 20th century almost one-third of adult men were Buddhist monks. The Qing dynasty absorbed the country in the 17th century. Mongolia declared independence after the Qing collapsed in 1911 and achieved actual independence from the Republic of China in 1921, shortly after which it became a satellite state of the Soviet Union. The Mongolian People's Republic was founded as a socialist state in 1924.

After the anti-communist revolutions of 1989, Mongolia carried out its own peaceful democratic revolution in 1990, which led to a multi-party system, a new constitution in 1992 and a market economy. It is a semi-presidential democratic republic with a unicameral legislature, the State Great Khural, of 126 seats. The 2024 population was 3,544,835, and roughly half live in Ulaanbaatar.
About 30 per cent of the population is nomadic or semi-nomadic, and horse culture remains integral. Mahayana Buddhism is the majority religion, at 51.7 per cent. The traditional dwelling is the ger.
montana: Montana is a landlocked state in the Mountain West of the western United States, with an area of 147,040 square miles. It is the fourth-largest state and the only one to border three Canadian provinces: British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The Continental Divide splits much of the state into distinct eastern and western regions. Most of its hundred or more named mountain ranges lie in the western half, which is part of the northern Rocky Mountains, while about 60 per cent of the state is prairie.

For thousands of years various indigenous peoples have lived in what is now Montana. Tribes met by Europeans and settlers from the United States included the Crow in the south-central area, the Cheyenne and Lakota in the southeast, the Blackfeet, Assiniboine and Gros Ventres in the central and north-central area, and the Kootenai and Salish in the west. Early Spanish explorers called the whole mountainous region of the west Montaña del Norte, from which the name derives.

Most of Montana came under American sovereignty with the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 and was explored by the Lewis and Clark Expedition soon after. Fur trappers followed and were the main economic activity until gold was discovered in 1858. The gold rush and the Homestead Acts of 1862 brought large numbers of American settlers. When Montana Territory was proposed in 1864, a representative objected that the name was a misnomer for a largely non-mountainous territory and that a Native American name would be better; the House Committee on Territories kept Montana.

Rapid growth led to statehood on 8 November 1889. Mining, particularly around Butte and Helena, remained the state's main economic engine through the mid-twentieth century. Montana granted women the vote in 1914, and in 1916 it became the first state to elect a woman to Congress, Jeannette Rankin.

Montana's capital is Helena and its most populous city is Billings. The state has no official nickname, but is known as Big Sky Country and the Treasure State. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture, with mining, oil, gas, coal and lumber also important. Glacier National Park and the site of the Battle of Little Bighorn are among its sights.
montevideo: Montevideo lies on the north shore of the Río de la Plata, the arm of the Atlantic Ocean that separates the south coast of Uruguay from the north coast of Argentina; Buenos Aires is 230 kilometres to the west on the Argentine side. The Bay of Montevideo forms a natural harbour, the largest in the country. The city's highest point is the peak of the Cerro de Montevideo, at 134 metres, crowned by a fortress. The name comes from this hill, though explanations of the second part differ: one holds that a sailor of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition cried out in Portuguese that he had seen a mount.

Portugal founded Colonia do Sacramento across the bay from Buenos Aires between 1680 and 1683, and met no resistance from the Spanish until 1723, when they began to fortify the heights around Montevideo Bay. On 22 November 1723 the Portuguese Field Marshal Manuel de Freitas da Fonseca built a fort there. Bruno Mauricio de Zabala, the Spanish governor of Buenos Aires, sent an expedition that forced the Portuguese to leave in 1724, and families from Buenos Aires and the Canary Islands settled. A census of 1724 counted more than 100 families of Galician and Canary Islands origin, more than 1,000 indigenous people, mostly Guaraní, and some enslaved people of Bantu origin.

No official document establishes the foundation, but Zabala's diary gives the date as 24 December 1726. The city won full independence from Buenos Aires only on 1 January 1730. It was briefly under British rule in 1807 before Spanish criollos, who had defeated the British invasions of the River Plate, retook it. From 1828 it belonged to Uruguay. By 1880 its population had quadrupled, mainly through European immigration.

Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay, with 1,287,452 people in the city proper in the 2023 census, about 36.8 per cent of the country's population. It is the country's chief port and its centre of commerce and higher education, and its University of the Republic was founded on 18 July 1849. It hosted every match of the first FIFA World Cup in 1930. Uruguayan tango originated in its neighbourhoods towards the end of the 1800s.
montreal: Montreal lies in the southwest of the province of Quebec. The city covers most of the Island of Montreal, at the confluence of the Saint Lawrence and Ottawa Rivers, between the Saint Lawrence to the south and the Rivière des Prairies to the north. It is 196 km east of Ottawa and 258 km southwest of Quebec City. Its port lies at one end of the Saint Lawrence Seaway, the river gateway that stretches from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. The most prominent feature of the island is Mount Royal, a mountain with three heads that rises 232 metres above sea level.

Archaeological evidence shows that First Nations peoples occupied the island as early as 4,000 years ago. By the year 1000 they had begun to cultivate maize, and within a few hundred years they had built fortified villages. The Saint Lawrence Iroquoians, a group distinct from the Haudenosaunee of present-day New York, established the village of Hochelaga at the foot of Mount Royal two centuries before the French arrived. The French explorer Jacques Cartier visited Hochelaga on 2 October 1535 and estimated its people at over a thousand. In the Mohawk language the land is called Tiohtià:ke, loosely where the group divided; in Ojibwe it is Mooniyaang, the first stopping place in the Ojibwe migration story.

Settlers from La Flèche in the Loire Valley founded the town in 1642 as Ville Marie, named for the Virgin Mary. The present name is generally thought to derive from Mount Royal, since réal and royal were used interchangeably in 16th-century French. Another explanation points to the Venetian geographer Giovanni Battista Ramusio, who wrote Monte Real on his 1556 map, but the Commission de toponymie du Québec disputes it. For over a century and a half Montreal was the industrial and financial centre of Canada, and Toronto surpassed it in population and economic strength in the 1970s.

French is the official language of Montreal, which is the largest primarily French speaking city in the Americas and one of the most bilingual in Canada. The city is divided into 19 boroughs, many of which were independent cities until a municipal reorganization in January 2002. It holds 50 National Historic Sites of Canada, more than any other city, many of them factories, warehouses and mills from its industrial past. Montreal hosted the 1967 International and Universal Exposition and the 1976 Summer Olympics, and is the headquarters of the International Civil Aviation Organization.
morocco: Morocco has coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, and covers about 446,300 km2. The Atlas Mountains run along the centre and south, the Rif Mountains lie in the north, and both ranges are mainly inhabited by Berber people. Most of the southeast lies in the Sahara Desert and is sparsely populated. The capital is Rabat, beside the Oued Bou Regreg River, and the largest city is the port of Casablanca. The English name Morocco comes from the Spanish Marruecos, itself derived from the name of Marrakesh, the capital of the Almoravid dynasty, the Almohad Caliphate and the Saadian dynasty.

People have lived in the region since the Paleolithic. Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud were dated to roughly 315,000 years ago. At Oued Beht a Neolithic farming society of 3400–2900 BCE formed the largest known agricultural complex in Africa outside the Nile Valley at that time. Phoenicians later established trading colonies, the most substantial being Chellah, Lixus and Mogador.

The Moroccan state traces its origins to the Idrisid dynasty founded by Idris I in 788. It reached its height as a regional power in the 11th and 12th centuries under the Berber Almoravid and Almohad dynasties, which controlled the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the Maghreb. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portugal seized some territory, but the Marinid and Saadi dynasties resisted foreign domination, and Morocco was the only North African nation to escape Ottoman rule. The Alawi dynasty, which still reigns, seized power in 1631. France and Spain established protectorates in 1912, and Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V.

Morocco is a unitary semi-constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament of two chambers, and the 2011 constitutional reforms reduced the king's executive powers and enlarged the prime minister's. The king remains Commander of the Faithful and holds wide powers over the military, foreign policy and religious affairs. The population was about 37 million in the 2024 census. Arabic and Tamazight are the official languages, and Islam is the official religion.
moscow: Moscow lies on the Moskva River, which flows for about 500 kilometres through the East European Plain in Central Russia, and 49 bridges span the river and its canals within the city. The city's name is thought to derive from the river's. The best-grounded theory traces it to a Proto-Balto-Slavic root meaning 'wet', so that Moskva would mean a river at a marsh. A Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, 'Black River'.

The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and around 950 CE two Slavic tribes, the Vyatichi and Krivichi, settled there. Chronicles first mention Moscow in 1147, as a minor town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal and a meeting place for Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich. It was fortified in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built, and was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237–1238 after the destruction of Ryazan.

The Grand Principality of Moscow led the unification of Russian lands in the 15th century, and the Kremlin was rebuilt then, with towers and churches by Italian architects. After the Tsardom of Russia was proclaimed in 1547, Moscow remained its political and economic centre until Peter the Great moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg in 1712. The capital returned to Moscow in 1918, after the establishment of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.

Moscow had 13,010,112 residents in the 2021 census, up from 11,503,501 in 2010. It is a federal city, divided into 12 administrative okrugs and 125 districts. Its road system radiates from the Kremlin and crosses circular roads that began as lines of fortification, among them the Boulevard Ring, on the line of the 16th-century wall of Bely Gorod, and the Garden Ring.

The Moscow Metro opened in 1935, and its original stations were decorated to impress and instruct the population. The city also holds Lomonosov Moscow State University, founded in 1755, and the Tretyakov Gallery, which has works by the icon painter Andrei Rublev.
moses: According to the Book of Exodus, Moses was born to Amram, a descendant of Kehath the Levite, and Jochebed, when the Israelites were an enslaved minority in Egypt. He had an older sister, Miriam, and an older brother, Aaron. Pharaoh had ordered all newborn Hebrew boys drowned in the Nile, so his mother hid him in an ark among the bulrushes, and Pharaoh's daughter adopted him. After he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, Moses fled to Midian and married Zipporah. On Mount Horeb God appeared to him as a burning bush and commanded him to bring the Israelites out of bondage. The Egyptian root msy, child of, as in Thutmose, has been proposed as the origin of his name.

After God sent ten plagues Pharaoh relented, and Moses led the Exodus across the Red Sea, where Pharaoh's army was destroyed. At Mount Sinai he received the Ten Commandments. After 40 years of wandering in the desert he died on Mount Nebo at the age of 120, within sight of the Promised Land.

Scholars disagree about his historicity. William G. Dever describes the modern consensus as that the biblical Moses is largely mythical, while allowing that a Moses-like figure may have lived in the southern Transjordan in the mid to late 13th century BCE. No Egyptian source mentions him before the fourth century BCE, and no archaeological evidence in Egypt or Sinai supports the story. Others hold that his leadership is too firmly rooted in Israel's collective memory to be pious fiction.

Jewish tradition considers Moses the foremost prophet, though Judaism stresses that he was a human being and not to be worshipped. He is also a major prophet in Samaritanism, Christianity and Islam. Hecataeus of Abdera, in the fourth century BCE, wrote the earliest reference to him in Greek literature. The Sistine Chapel has six frescoes of his life, painted in 1481-82 by artists including Sandro Botticelli and Pietro Perugino. Because the Hebrew word keren can mean horn or ray, Jerome's Latin Vulgate describes his face as horned, and Western art until the Renaissance often shows him with small horns, as in Michelangelo's statue of 1513 to 1515.
moskva-river: The river rises about 140 kilometres west of Moscow, crosses Smolensk and Moscow Oblasts and reaches the Oka about 110 kilometres south-east of the capital. Its length is given as 473 kilometres, or by another measure 502, its basin covers 17,600 square kilometres, and it falls 155 metres along its course. An estimated 61 per cent of its water comes from thaw, 12 per cent from rain and 27 per cent from underground sources. It normally freezes around November or December and begins to thaw in late March. On its banks, besides Moscow, stand Mozhaysk, Zvenigorod, Zhukovsky, Bronnitsy and Voskresensk.

Recent studies suggest that the river has occupied its present bed for about 12,000 years. Finnic peoples lived along it, as did Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi. The name of the city is thought to come from that of the river. The most widely accepted explanation derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root connected with wetness, so that it may have meant a river in a marsh or wetland. One Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, black river. To tell the two apart, Russians usually call the river Moskva-reka.

The first stone bridge across it, the Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, was built in 1692. The Vodootvodny Canal, dug in the 1780s, created the island opposite the Kremlin that Muscovites informally call Bolotny Ostrov, Bog Island. Dams built in 1785, 1836 and 1878 failed to keep the river navigable through summer droughts. The highest recorded water level in central Moscow, 127.25 metres above sea level against a usual 120, was reached in the flood of 1908.

Since the Moscow Canal was completed, in 1932–1937, the river has also carried a share of water from the upper Volga, which has made commercial shipping reliable. The average discharge, Volga water included, rises from 38 cubic metres a second near Zvenigorod to 250 at the mouth. As of 2007 there were 49 bridges over the river and its canals within the city, where it is 120 to 200 metres wide and narrowest under the Kremlin walls. Moscow draws its drinking water from five stations on the river and from the upper Volga reservoirs. The stretch within the city freezes only occasionally, on account of contamination.
mount-everest: Mount Everest lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas, and its summit marks part of the China–Nepal border. A joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities in 2020 measured its height as 8,848.86 metres above sea level. Because that height is taken from the geoid, which approximates sea level, climbers ascend only part of it; the nearest sea, the Bay of Bengal, is almost 700 kilometres away. The mountain has an ice cap climate, with every month averaging well below freezing, and very little native life: a moss grows at 6,480 metres, and a small black jumping spider has been found as high as 6,700 metres.

The Nepali name is Sagarmāthā, literally 'head in the sky'. The Tibetan name Qomolangma means 'holy mother'; it was first recorded in a Chinese transcription in the 1721 Kangxi Atlas and reached the West in 1733 on a map by the French geographer D'Anville. The official Chinese form is a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan, adopted after a decree of May 1952 that chose a single name.

In 1802 the British began the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India to fix the positions, heights and names of the world's highest mountains. The teams, using theodolites that each weighed 500 kilograms and needed 12 men to carry, reached the Himalayan foothills by the 1830s. Nepal, suspicious of British intentions, refused their requests to enter, so the surveyors worked from the Terai to the south, where torrential rain and malaria killed three survey officers and forced two others to retire.

Nepal also barred foreigners from climbing, so the first recorded attempts were British expeditions on the North Ridge from Tibet. The reconnaissance of 1921 reached 7,000 metres on the North Col. In 1922 climbers went above 8,000 metres for the first time, reaching 8,321 metres. On 8 June 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine made a final summit attempt and never returned, and it remains debated whether they reached the top. Tenzing Norgay, who had reached 8,595 metres with the Swiss expedition of 1952, made the first documented ascent in 1953 with Edmund Hillary by the Southeast Ridge.

Only about 200 people had reached the summit by 1987. Large national expeditions were the norm until commercial expeditions began in the 1990s. The mountain's dangers include winds beyond 320 kilometres an hour when the jet stream descends, blizzards and avalanches. Climbers usually start from base camps above 5,000 metres; on the Nepalese side they fly to Lukla and trek to the South Base Camp, while on the Tibetan side most drive to the North Base Camp. Nepal and Tibet each manage climbing through permits.
mozambique: Mozambique lies on the southeast coast of Africa, bordered by the Indian Ocean, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and South Africa. The Zambezi River divides it into two topographical regions. North of the river a narrow coastal strip gives way to inland hills, low plateaus and rugged highlands covered with miombo woodlands. South of it the lowlands are broader. The climate is tropical, with a wet season from October to March and a dry season from April to September.

The country was named Moçambique by the Portuguese after the Island of Mozambique. The island's name is derived from Musa ibn Bique, an Arab trader who first visited it, later lived there and was its ruler when Vasco da Gama called in 1498. The island-town was the capital of the Portuguese colony until 1898, when the capital moved south to Lourenço Marques, now Maputo.

Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into Southeast Africa as early as the 4th century BCE. Between the 1st and 5th centuries CE waves of migration passed through the Zambezi valley into the plateau and coastal areas. They established agricultural communities and herding societies and brought the technology of iron smelting and smithing. From the late first millennium CE, Indian Ocean trade networks reached as far south as the port town of Chibuene. From the 9th century, port towns grew along the East African coast and shared in an incipient Swahili culture. Islam was often adopted by urban elites, which facilitated trade.

Sofala, Angoche and Mozambique Island were regional powers by the 15th century. Inland states such as the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa Empire supplied gold and ivory, which were exchanged up the coast to larger ports such as Kilwa and Mombasa. Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1498 marked the Portuguese entry into the region. They gained control of the Island of Mozambique and of Sofala in the early 16th century, and by the 1530s traders and prospectors seeking gold had set up garrisons and trading posts at Sena and Tete on the Zambezi. Portuguese posts and forts displaced Arab commercial and military dominance.

Mozambique is the Republic of Mozambique, a presidential republic with its capital and largest city at Maputo. It became independent in 1975 after more than four centuries of Portuguese rule, and a civil war followed from 1977 to 1992. Portuguese is the only official language, alongside local languages such as Tsonga, Makhuwa and Sena. The Makonde are known for their wood carving and masks, and the Chopi for their marimba music and dance.
muhammad: The early sources for Muhammad's life are Muslim authors of the 8th and 9th centuries CE, and scholars dispute how far they can be trusted because of the gap between his life and their writing. Western historians describe the early biographies as written largely to convey a message rather than to record history exactly. What follows is the traditional account.

According to it, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, the leading tribe of western Arabia. His father Abdullah died around the time of his birth and his mother Amina when he was six, and his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib brought him up. At 25 he married Khadija, a wealthy woman of 40. He would withdraw for nights of prayer to a mountain cave named Hira, where, at about 40, around 610, he reported that the angel Gabriel gave him his first revelation from God.

In 613 Muhammad began to preach publicly that God is One and that complete submission, Islam, to God is the right way of life. His followers were few and were persecuted by Meccan polytheists for 13 years. In 622 he and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, then called Yathrib. This migration, the Hijrah, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina he united the tribes under the Constitution of Medina.

After years of intermittent fighting with Meccan tribes, he marched on Mecca in 630 with 10,000 converts and seized the city with minimal casualties. He declared an amnesty for past offences, except for ten men and women, and had the statues of Arabian gods in and around the Kaaba destroyed. By his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.

Muhammad fell ill in June 632 and died on 8 June in the house of his wife Aisha, where he was buried. A dispute over succession followed. Umar ibn al-Khattab nominated Abu Bakr, who was confirmed as the first caliph, while some companions held that Muhammad had designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib. Within a decade Muslims conquered Mesopotamia, Byzantine Syria and Egypt and large parts of Persia. Muslims hold that he was the last prophet sent by God and that his revelations form the Quran. His sayings and practices, preserved in the hadith, make up the sunnah, which supplies many details of prayer, fasting and pilgrimage not found in the Quran.
muhammad-al-amin-bey: Born on 4 September 1881, he married Lalla Jeneïna Beya, the daughter of a Tripolitanian merchant of Tunis, in 1902. On 25 June 1942 Moncef Bey named him Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent. A month later he warned Moncef that the court counsellor General M'hammed Belkhodja was urging the French Resident General Jean-Pierre Esteva to depose him.

In May 1943 General Alphonse Juin came to Tunis with orders to remove Moncef Bey for alleged attempts to collaborate with the Axis forces. Juin found no grounds for condemning him. Lamine at first refused to promise that he would accept the throne and agreed largely because of the benefits to his family. Juin installed him at the Bardo palace on 15 May 1943. Moncef abdicated only on 6 July.

For most Tunisians he remained a usurper, the Bey of the French. The other Husainid princes boycotted him. The death of Moncef Bey in exile on 1 September 1948 removed the possibility of a restoration, and his subjects began to regard him as their legitimate ruler.

He then worked clandestinely with Habib Bourguiba and Salah Ben Youssef for self-government. In 1952 the Resident General Jean de Hauteclocque imprisoned Bourguiba and had the Bey's ministers arrested; the Bey refused to sign decrees, bringing government to a standstill, and gave way after the trade union leader Farhat Hached was assassinated in December 1952. In 1954 he accepted a reform package negotiated by Muhammad Salah Mzali while Bourguiba was still confined. After the French Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France announced internal autonomy on 31 July 1954, France dealt with the Neo Destour alone.

As king he signed without protest the decree of 31 May 1956 that abolished the privileges of the ruling family. On 15 July 1957 the Tunisian army replaced the Royal Guard around the palace, and on 25 July the Constituent Assembly voted by a show of hands to abolish the monarchy.

He was taken with members of his family to an abandoned palace in Manouba without water or electricity; two of his sons and his son-in-law were imprisoned. In October 1958 he and his wife were moved to a small villa in La Soukra, still under house arrest. She died two days after three days of interrogation about the family jewels, and his confinement was then lifted. He died in Tunis on 30 September 1962 and was buried beside her in the cemetery of Sidi Abdelaziz in La Marsa, not in the dynasty's mausoleum of Tourbet el Bey.
muhammad-shaybani: Muhammad Shaybani was a Shaybanid, a descendant of Shiban, son of Jochi Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan. His father was Budaq Sultan, one of the eleven sons of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, ruler of the Uzbek ulus, and his mother was Aq Quzi Begum. According to the historian Kamal ad-Din Binai, his father nicknamed him Shibägh, wormwood. Budaq Sultan was an educated man who had Persian works translated into Turkic, and Shaybani was fluent in both languages. He was fond of history in his youth, and in 1475 was presented with the Alexander Romance of Nizami Ganjavi.

He first appears leading 3,000 men in the army of the Timurid ruler of Samarkand, Sultan Ahmed Mirza. When Ahmed went to war with Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan over Tashkent, Shaybani secretly agreed with the Moghul khan to betray and plunder Ahmed's army, which he did at the Battle of the Chirciq River in 1488. Mahmud Khan rewarded him with Turkistan. There he oppressed the local Kazakhs, which led to a war between Moghulistan and the Kazakh Khanate that Moghulistan lost, while Shaybani's standing among the Uzbeks grew.

He ousted the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500, retook it in 1501, conquered Bukhara the same year and founded the Shaybanid dynasty of the Khanate of Bukhara. He fought successfully against Babur, later founder of the Mughal Empire, and married Babur's sister Khanzada Begum; Babur's freedom to leave Samarkand depended on his consent. He aligned himself with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II against the Shia Safavids. He patronised the Yemeni religious figure known as Mir-i Arab and wrote religious and philosophical works in Chagatai, among them the Bahr ul-Khudo of 1508. Raids on Kazakh lands in 1508–09 ended in a major defeat by Kasym Khan in 1510.

In 1510 Ismail I invaded western Khorasan. Shaybani had lost most of his cavalry in a campaign against the Hazaras, so he withdrew behind the walls of Merv. Ismail besieged the city for a month without result and then feigned a retreat. According to some sources the khan's emirs advised waiting for reinforcements, but his wife Aisha Sultan Khanum shamed the council into fighting. His army was surrounded by Ismail's 17,000 men and destroyed, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape, on 2 December 1510. Shaybani was succeeded by an uncle, a cousin and a brother, whose descendants ruled Bukhara until 1598 and Khwarezm until 1687.
mukunda-deva: Mukunda Deva, also called Mukunda Harichandana, traced his descent from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, and the traditions of Odisha call him Telinga Mukundadeva. His Bhimeswara temple inscription names his father as Saravaraju and his grandfather as Singaraju. He took the throne at Kataka in 1559 after killing Raghuram Raya Chotaraya, the last ruler of the Bhoi dynasty, and is counted as the founder and only monarch of a Chalukya dynasty of Odisha.

As king he tried to revive the power of Odisha. He laid out two streets from the Lion's Gateway to the Gundicha Temple and made the road smooth by filling its pits and holes. On the outer side of the southern walls he raised a swing arch, the Dola Mandap, on which the deities are swung during the Dola festival in the last five days of the month of Falguna. He also built a chain of forts at Raibania, in the present Balasore district.

His foreign relations were shaped by two powers: the Sultan of Bengal, his enemy, and the Mughal emperor Akbar, his ally. In 1560 Sultan Ghiyasuddin Jalal Shah of Bengal invaded and marched as far as Jajpur, and Mukunda Deva defeated him and drove him out.

In 1567, while Akbar was occupied with the invasion of Chittorgarh, the Karrani sultan of Bengal invaded. Mukunda Deva was defeated and took shelter in the fort of Kotsima, and the Bengal army under the general Kalapahada made a devastating attack on the capital, Cuttack. In the king's absence Ramachandra Bhanja, a feudatory of Sarangagarh, declared himself king. Mukunda Deva hurried back and met him in battle at Gohiratikiri, near Jajpur, where Mukunda Deva was killed.

Ramachandra Bhanja was himself later executed by the sultan's forces. Afterwards Ramachandra Deva I of the Bhoi dynasty, son of Danai Vidyadhara, allied himself with Akbar to avoid an Afghan invasion and continued to rule as a subordinate king of Odisha.
mumbai: Mumbai lies on the Konkan coast of western India, on a narrow peninsula of Salsette Island bounded by the Arabian Sea, Thane Creek and Vasai Creek, at the mouth of the Ulhas River. It has a deep natural harbour. The city grew from an archipelago of seven islands: the Isle of Bombay, Parel, Mazagaon, Mahim, Colaba, Worli and Old Woman's Island, also called Little Colaba. Greater Mumbai covers 603 square kilometres in two districts, Mumbai City, the southern Island City, and Mumbai Suburban.

The islands were inhabited since the South Asian Stone Age. They became part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, followed by the Satavahana dynasty in the 2nd century BCE, and Ptolemy mentioned them in 150 CE. The Koli fishing community, whose goddess Mumbadevi is believed to have given the city its name, settled the region around the beginning of the Common Era. The Delhi Sultanate and then the Gujarat Sultanate ruled them in the Middle Ages. The islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535 and in 1661 passed to the British Crown, which leased them to the East India Company in 1668.

Under British rule Bombay became the capital of the Bombay Presidency and a major trading and administrative centre. The Hornby Vellard project, begun in 1782 and completed in 1845, reclaimed land between the seven islands from the Arabian Sea and unified them. With new roads and railways and the cotton boom of the 19th century, it made the city a major seaport. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation was established in 1888. The city played a major part in the Indian independence movement. After 1947 it became the capital of Bombay State, and after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement the capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra and the financial and commercial capital of India. Its population was 12,442,373 at the 2011 census, with more than 18 million in the metropolitan region. Its buildings from the British period, such as Victoria Terminus, are largely in the Gothic Revival style, while the Gateway of India is Indo-Saracenic and Marine Drive has many Art Deco buildings. The city is also the centre of Bollywood, the Hindi film industry, whose name blends Bombay and Hollywood.
munich: Munich lies on the elevated plains of Upper Bavaria, in the Northern Alpine Foreland, about 50 kilometres north of the Alps and about 520 metres above sea level. The rivers Isar and Würm flow through the city. The northern part of the plateau is a fertile flint area, the southern part is covered with morainic hills, and between them lie outwash plains where groundwater rising through the gravel has formed marshes in the north.
The name goes back to a tiny monastic settlement of the 10th century called zu den Munchen, 'to the monks'; the Old High German Munche is the base of the modern München.

The Isar was a prehistoric trade route, and in the Bronze Age Munich was among the largest raft ports in Europe; settlements up to four thousand years old have been found, along with Celtic settlements of the Iron Age. The Roman road Via Julia, linking Augsburg and Salzburg, crossed the Isar south of the city. From the 6th century the Baiuvarii settled the area, and the first known Christian church was built in Fröttmanning around 815. Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, founded the town to control the salt trade after burning down Föhring and its bridges over the Isar; historians date this to about 1158.

Munich remained Catholic during the Reformation and became the capital of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. Its population, only 24,000 in 1700, doubled about every 30 years: 100,000 in 1852, 250,000 in 1883 and 500,000 in 1901. The House of Wittelsbach ruled until 1918, when the German revolution of 1918–1919 ended its reign and brought the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic. In the 1920s the city became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the Nazi Party, and it was known as the Capital of the Movement. Munich was heavily bombed in the Second World War, though much of its historic architecture has since been restored. It passed one million inhabitants in 1957 and hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

Munich is the capital of Bavaria and the third-largest city in Germany, with about 1.5 million inhabitants. It is the seat of the Bavarian Landtag and of institutions such as the Federal Finance Court and the European Patent Office. The old town centres on the Marienplatz, with the Old Town Hall and the New Town Hall, and includes the Frauenkirche, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising, and the Michaelskirche. Nymphenburg Palace was begun in 1664, the Englischer Garten was laid out between 1789 and 1807, and the city is known for the annual Oktoberfest.
mustafa-kemal-ataturk: Shortly after graduating from military school he was arrested for activities against the regime of Sultan Abdul Hamid II, and he was released after months only with the support of his former school director. He was posted to the Fifth Army in Damascus as a staff captain, joined a small secret society of reformist officers called Vatan ve Hürriyet, and later joined the Committee of Union and Progress, though he became known for his criticism of its leaders.

He took part in the suppression of a tribal rebellion in Tripolitania in 1908 and in the suppression of the counter-revolution of April 1909, the 31 March Incident, which ended with the deposition of Abdul Hamid II. He fought in the Italo-Turkish and Balkan Wars and rose to prominence in the Defence of Gallipoli during the First World War. After the Ottoman defeat he directed the Turkish National Movement against the partition of the country by the victorious powers, set up the provisional Ankara government and won the war against Greece, Armenia, France and the United Kingdom, a result confirmed in the Treaty of Lausanne.

During and after the war the ethnic cleansing of Armenians and Greeks from Anatolia outside Istanbul was largely completed through massacres, flight, expulsions and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. His government abolished the Ottoman sultanate in 1922 and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923, with Atatürk as its first president until his death on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, aged 57. He was succeeded by İsmet İnönü.

As president he sought complete independence, which he defined as economic, financial, juridical, military and cultural. He led reforms to build a republican and secular nation-state with a Western facing society. The Ottoman Caliphate was abolished, a fully secular civil code replaced the semi-secular Mecelle, the fez was banned, thousands of schools were opened and a Latin-based Turkish alphabet was introduced. State-owned enterprises were set up and the first five-year plan was begun. Turkish women received equal civil and political rights.
